sections.html:
Warrensburg is both the seat and the largest city of Johnson County, a western Missouri county bordering Lafayette, Pettis, Henry, Cass and Jackson counties and tied into the wider Kansas City area. Holden and Knob Noster round out the cities. In 2025 the county counted 56,670 residents, 4.9% more than in 2020. Owners live in 63.5% of homes. The typical owned home is valued at $235,700, and typical gross rent is $932.

Seven public school districts cover the county, and each adds a levy to bills inside its boundaries. Buyers will want to know which one serves your house.

Responsibility splits three ways. Value and the owner of record are the Assessor's job. Each taxing district picks its own rate. Billing, payment and the hand-off of funds to those districts belong to the Collector.

  • Assessor: Johnson County South Annex, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite B, Warrensburg, MO 64093, phone 660-747-9822.
  • Collector: 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A, Warrensburg, MO 64093, phone 660-747-5531.
  • Thanksgiving: county administrative offices will be closed on Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27, 2026.

The Assessor has no role in rates, collections or what schools and fire districts receive. If you wonder why a levy went up, ask the district that charges it.

sections.h2: How market value becomes a tax bill
sections.html:
The county publishes its formula. Multiply market value by the adjustment factor for the property class to get assessed value, divide by 100, multiply by a district's rate, and total the districts.

Johnson County assessment factors
Property classShare of market value assessed
Residential19%
Commercial32%
Agricultural12%

Which districts apply depends on where your parcel lies: school, fire, ambulance and city.

Real estate values are redone in odd-numbered years under Missouri law, and the next round is 2027. A jump of $500 or more in assessed value triggers a mailed Change in Assessed Value Notice, usually in June, and even-numbered years can bring one too. Since no tax estimate is included, call the Assessor if you want one.

The county outlines three steps. First, read the notice for factual errors. Second, if you have proof of a different value or of a data mistake, ask the Assessor for an informal hearing. Third, when that goes nowhere, submit a Property Assessment Appeal Form to get in front of the Board of Equalization. Hearings are by appointment, and contact details are printed on every mailed notice.

Filing with the Board closes on the second Monday of July (July 12 in 2027). The Assessor or County Clerk can tell you where the form goes and whether any extension applies. If the Board rules against you, the State Tax Commission is next, and you have 30 days counted from the date of the decision letter.

  • You may owe the tax while an appeal is pending, and balances left after December 31 accrue interest and penalties.
  • Signing a value agreement with the Assessor during a Board appeal settles the matter for good, with no Commission appeal after it.
  • Appeals to the Commission by an LLC, trust, estate or corporation need an attorney.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to find your balance
sections.html:
Bills leave the Collector's office in late October. Delinquency starts after December 31, so mailed checks must bear a postmark of that day or sooner. Envelopes with a later postmark come back unprocessed, unless the late fees are enclosed.

Your balance is on the county's Search Taxes page. Choose Real Estate and type in a name, street address or mailing address; the first number returned is your parcel number. Under Missouri statute 140.100, land in the back tax book takes an 18 percent penalty for each year of delinquency, so a lapsed bill climbs quickly.

Escrowed owners get new figures through their mortgage company, but the county notes that getting the bill paid on time is still the owner's duty.

Ordinance 25-01, passed by the County Commission on March 17, 2025, set up a Senior Real Estate Tax Credit under section 137.1050. It is open to homeowners age 62 and over and applies to the primary residence, measured by how much tax rises after a starting credit year.

  • The application period has been April 1 to June 30. The Collector can tell you when the next one begins.
  • Not covered: agricultural and commercial property, personal property, voter-approved bond levies and the State Blind Pension levy.
  • Every tax on the homestead has to be paid up.
  • Your value is not frozen; reassessment still happens in odd years.

Sellers should know the credit follows the person. A buyer does not inherit it, and a homeowner who buys elsewhere starts over with a new application and a new starting year.

Three years behind puts a parcel on the list for the yearly tax certificate sale, which takes place on the fourth Monday of August, 10 a.m., at 301 W Market Street in Warrensburg. Notice of the list runs in a local newspaper for three weeks before that.

What a bidder gets is a tax lien and no ownership. Redemption is open to the owner of record and to anyone with a recorded lien or deed of trust, for one year and then until a collector's deed is issued. The price is the bid plus 10% annual interest, and 8% on later years' tax the buyer covered. If 18 months pass after the sale with no collector's deed, the buyer's lien is gone.

Any surplus above the opening bid is held by the County Treasurer. To claim it, an owner or lienholder has ninety days after redemption ends to file with the county commission; after that it goes to the schools.

A tax balance alone will not stop a sale, because the title company can ask for a payoff figure and take it out of your proceeds. Here is the order of work.

  1. Phone the Collector, 660-747-5531, and request a payoff figure with penalty and interest built in.
  2. A house more than a year behind should have that figure in hand before it is listed.
  3. A house close to three years behind is the urgent case, since it can land in the August sale.
  4. Hand the written figure to the title company so the settlement statement matches it.

A cash sale can close fast enough to pay the arrears before the sale date, and the proceeds cover the bill the same way they would in any other closing.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Johnson County real estate tax?
faqs.a: At the Collector's office, 1310 S Maguire St, Suite A in Warrensburg, or through the county's online payment link. The phone is 660-747-5531. A mailed payment needs a December 31 postmark.

faqs.q: What is the Johnson County residential assessment rate?
faqs.a: Nineteen percent of market value. Commercial property is 32% and agricultural property is 12%. District rates then apply to that assessed value.

faqs.q: When will Johnson County reassess my house again?
faqs.a: In 2027, because Missouri reassesses real estate in odd-numbered years. If assessed value rises by $500 or more, a notice usually comes by mail in June.

faqs.q: Does the Johnson County senior tax credit pass to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. It stays with the applicant. A buyer who is 62 or older would need a new application, and a seller who moves must apply again for the new home.

faqs.q: How long before Johnson County sells a home for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: A parcel with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale on the fourth Monday in August. The owner can redeem during the next year by paying the bid plus 10% annual interest.
